name: Losar
summary: Losar is the Tibetan new year, on the first day of the first lunar month. In East Sikkim it is felt most at Rumtek and the Tibetan and Bhutia households of Gangtok: prayers, butter lamps, fresh prayer flags, khapse biscuits and family visits over several days.
body: Losar opens the Tibetan lunar year and usually falls in February or early March. Rumtek has a special tie to the day: the 16th Karmapa, Rangjung Rigpe Dorje, formally inaugurated the rebuilt monastery as his seat in exile on Losar in 1966, after fleeing Tibet in 1959. Monks clean the halls, renew prayer flags and offerings, and hold prayers in the days around the new year.

In Gangtok, Tibetan and Bhutia families spend the first days at home and in visits to relatives. Kitchens fry khapse, twisted biscuits made for the season, and there is chhang and butter tea for guests. Many shops in Lal Bazaar and on MG Marg run short hours or close for a day or two, so plan meals and shopping around that.

For visitors, Losar is a quiet, domestic festival more than a show. Go to Rumtek in the morning, stay on the edge of the courtyard, and ask before photographing monks at prayer. Late February is also cold and dry in Gangtok, around 4–14 °C, with clear mornings for the Kangchenjunga range and snow likely higher up at Tsomgo.
tips: Losar dates move each year with the lunar calendar; check the date for your year before you book.
Dress modestly for monastery visits, remove shoes where asked and walk clockwise around stupas and prayer wheels.
Book Gangtok rooms early if Losar falls on a long weekend, and expect some restaurants to close for a day or two.

faqs.q: When is Losar celebrated in Sikkim
faqs.a: Losar falls on the first day of the first month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, which lands in February or early March. The exact date changes every year, so check a current calendar or ask your hotel. Celebrations run over several days, with the first two or three days the most important for families and monasteries.

faqs.q: Can tourists attend Losar at Rumtek Monastery
faqs.a: Yes, visitors can usually enter Rumtek during the Losar period, though some halls may be closed during private rituals. Carry photo ID, as there is a security check at the gate. Keep voices low, dress modestly and ask before taking photos. Arrive in the morning, when prayers are under way and the light on the courtyard is soft.

faqs.q: Is Losar the same as Losoong
faqs.a: No. Losar is the Tibetan new year in February or March. Losoong, or Sonam Losoong, is the Sikkimese harvest new year of the Bhutia people, held on the first day of the eleventh lunar month, usually in December. The Lepchas celebrate it as Namsoong. Both involve prayers, food and family visits, but they fall at different times of year.

faqs.q: What is the weather like in Gangtok during Losar
faqs.a: Expect cold, mostly dry weather. Gangtok typically sits around 4–14 °C in February, with clear mornings and chilly nights. Tsomgo Lake may still be frozen and the Nathu La road can close after snowfall, so keep a spare day if those are on your list, and check current status before you travel.

name: Saga Dawa
when: May–Jun, full moon of the fourth Tibetan month
summary: Saga Dawa is the holiest month of the Tibetan Buddhist year, marking the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and passing. Its full-moon day is a Sikkim holiday, when monks carry sacred texts through Gangtok in a procession and monasteries hold butter-lamp prayers.
body: The fourth month of the Tibetan calendar, Saga Dawa, is set aside to remember three events in the Buddha's life: his birth, his enlightenment and his parinirvana. Buddhists believe merit made during this month is multiplied, so many people avoid meat, give to charity and visit monasteries more often. The full-moon day, Saga Dawa Duchen, usually falls in late May or June and is a public holiday in Sikkim.

In Gangtok the day is marked by a procession in which monks and lay people carry the holy scriptures through the streets, with drums, horns and incense. Monasteries across the town hold prayers, and butter lamps are lit through the evening. Families also release fish and birds as an act of merit.

For travellers, the timing overlaps with the end of the pre-monsoon season. Mornings can still be clear, but afternoon showers are common by June, and NH10 can start to see landslides. It is also a busy domestic holiday period, so book rooms ahead and keep a buffer day on either side of long drives.
tips: Watch the procession from the pavement and let it pass; do not cut through the line or walk in front of the scriptures.
Many Buddhists eat vegetarian food during Saga Dawa, so you will find more vegetarian momos and thukpa than usual.
June arrivals should check NH10 status the day before travel, as early monsoon landslides can delay the drive from Siliguri.

faqs.q: When is Saga Dawa in 2026 and 2027
faqs.a: Saga Dawa Duchen is the full-moon day of the fourth Tibetan month. It usually falls between late May and late June, and the exact date changes every year with the lunar calendar. Check the Sikkim government holiday list for the year of your trip, as the full-moon day is a state public holiday and many offices close.

faqs.q: What happens in Gangtok on Saga Dawa
faqs.a: Monks and lay devotees carry Buddhist scriptures through the town in a procession with drums, horns and incense. Monasteries hold prayers through the day and butter lamps are lit in the evening. It is a religious occasion rather than a fair, so there are no ticketed events. Visitors are welcome to watch quietly from the roadside.

faqs.q: Is Saga Dawa a good time to visit Gangtok
faqs.a: It can be. Late May and early June bring warm days, around 15–24 °C in Gangtok, and the festival adds a quiet, devotional feel to the town. The downside is weather: showers increase in June, mountain views are less reliable and NH10 landslides become more likely. Book early, as Indian school holidays push hotel prices up.

faqs.q: Do shops close in Gangtok for Saga Dawa
faqs.a: Government offices and banks close on the full-moon holiday, and some shops keep shorter hours, especially around the procession route. MG Marg cafes and most hotels stay open. Carry some cash in case smaller shops are shut.

name: Pang Lhabsol
when: Aug–Sep, 15th day of the seventh Tibetan month
summary: Pang Lhabsol honours Mount Kangchenjunga as Sikkim's guardian deity and recalls the brotherhood pact between Lepcha and Bhutia leaders. In Gangtok the main celebration is at Tsuklakhang, the royal chapel, with masked dances and the Pangtoed warrior dance.
body: Pang Lhabsol is unique to Sikkim. It falls on the fifteenth day of the seventh Tibetan month, in late August or September, and offers worship to Kangchenjunga, the mountain the Sikkimese regard as their protector. Tradition holds that the festival also remembers a blood-brotherhood pact sworn between the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek and Khye Bumsa, ancestor of the Namgyal kings, with the mountain's spirits called as witnesses.

The festival was popularised by the third Chogyal, Chakdor Namgyal, who ruled from 1700 to 1716. Tradition credits him with introducing the Pangtoed, the warrior dance, after a vision. At Tsuklakhang Palace in Gangtok, dancers in armour and helmets perform alongside masked monks, and Kangchenjunga itself is represented by a dancer in a red mask.

Expect the courtyard at Tsuklakhang to fill early with local families. The timing sits at the end of the monsoon, so roads may still be patchy and views of the real mountain are uncertain. Hotel rates are low in this season, which makes it a good-value trip if you have flexible days. Check current status of NH10 before you travel.
tips: Reach Tsuklakhang at least an hour before the dances start to find space at the edge of the courtyard.
Carry an umbrella and a light rain jacket: late August and September still bring heavy showers in Gangtok.
Ask locally for the exact programme each year, as timings for the dances are set by the monastery and can shift.

faqs.q: What is Pang Lhabsol and why is it celebrated
faqs.a: Pang Lhabsol is a Sikkimese festival that honours Mount Kangchenjunga as the guardian deity of Sikkim. Tradition says it also recalls a pact of blood brotherhood between the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek and the Bhutia ancestor Khye Bumsa. The third Chogyal, Chakdor Namgyal, popularised it in the early 18th century, and tradition credits him with the warrior dance.

faqs.q: Where can I watch Pang Lhabsol in Gangtok
faqs.a: The main celebration in Gangtok is at Tsuklakhang Palace, the royal chapel of the former Chogyals, near the Secretariat. Masked dances and the Pangtoed warrior dance are performed in the courtyard. Entry is free. Arrive early, as local families fill the space, and follow instructions from the monastery volunteers about where to stand.

faqs.q: When is Pang Lhabsol held
faqs.a: It falls on the fifteenth day of the seventh month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, usually in late August or September. The date changes each year. Sikkim declares it a state holiday, so you can confirm the date from the official holiday list for your year, and check with your hotel for dance timings at Tsuklakhang.

faqs.q: Is September a good time to visit Gangtok for Pang Lhabsol
faqs.a: It is good for value but not for guaranteed views. Late August and September still bring rain and occasional landslides on NH10, and Kangchenjunga is often hidden in cloud. In return, hotel rates are among the lowest of the year and crowds are thin until the Puja holidays in October. Keep a buffer day and check current status before you travel.

name: Kagyed Dance
when: Early December, 28th–29th day of the tenth Tibetan month
summary: Kagyed is a two-day masked dance at Tsuklakhang, the royal chapel in Gangtok, held in early December a few days before the Losoong new year. Monks in masks and brocade enact stories of Guru Padmasambhava, and the festival ends with the burning of effigies that stand for evil.
body: Kagyed is performed on the 28th and 29th days of the tenth month of the Tibetan calendar, which usually falls in early December. The main performance is in the shrine courtyard of Tsuklakhang Palace in Gangtok, and monasteries such as Phodong and Old Rumtek hold their own. The dances honour eight tantric deities and are meant to clear away the misfortunes of the passing year before the new one.

Monks in painted masks and long brocade robes move to the beat of drums, cymbals and long horns, acting out episodes from the life of Guru Padmasambhava. The mood is serious, but jesters break in between dances for comic relief, and children in the crowd wait for them. On the last day, effigies made of flour, wood and paper are carried out and burned.

Early December is one of the best times to be in Gangtok: dry, clear and cold, with the Kangchenjunga range sharp in the mornings. Hotels are quieter than in October, so rates soften. Pack warm layers, as Gangtok nights drop to around 4–6 °C, and the Tsomgo road may close after snow.
tips: Wear warm layers and carry a cushion or mat: you will sit or stand on cold stone for a couple of hours.
Do not step into the dance area or use flash; monks perform a religious rite, not a stage show.
Combine Kagyed with Losoong a few days later for a week that shows Sikkim's winter festival season.

faqs.q: When is the Kagyed dance in Gangtok
faqs.a: Kagyed falls on the 28th and 29th days of the tenth Tibetan lunar month, which usually lands in early December. The exact dates shift each year, so check with Sikkim Tourism or your hotel. The main performance is at Tsuklakhang Palace in Gangtok, and it takes place a few days before Losoong, the Sikkimese harvest new year.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for Kagyed at Tsuklakhang
faqs.a: No, there is normally no ticket. The dance is a religious performance in the palace monastery courtyard, and the public watch from around the edges. Space fills early, so arrive at least an hour ahead. Follow the volunteers' instructions about where to stand, and keep the dance area clear at all times.

faqs.q: What do the Kagyed dances mean
faqs.a: The dances honour eight tantric deities and depict stories from the life of Guru Padmasambhava, the teacher credited with bringing Buddhism to the Himalaya. Their purpose is to drive away misfortune before the new year. At the end, effigies representing evil are burned. Jesters perform between the main dances to lighten the mood.

faqs.q: How cold is Gangtok in early December
faqs.a: Expect around 5–15 °C in the day and colder nights, with dry, clear weather. Bring a warm jacket, a cap and good shoes. Higher up, Tsomgo Lake can be near freezing and snow may close the Nathu La road for a few days. Keep a buffer day for the passes and check current status before you travel.

name: Losoong
when: December, first day of the eleventh Tibetan month
summary: Losoong, also called Sonam Losoong, is the harvest new year of the Sikkimese Bhutia, held in December. The Lepchas celebrate it as Namsoong. Monasteries stage masked dances beforehand, effigies of evil are burned, and families gather for food, chhang and archery.
body: Losoong falls on the first day of the eleventh month of the Tibetan calendar, usually in December. It marks the end of the harvest, when farmers have stored their grain and can celebrate. It is a festival of the Bhutia people, adapted from the traditions of Losar, and the Lepchas mark it too under the name Namsoong. In Gangtok it follows close on the Kagyed dances at Tsuklakhang.

The festival is preceded by masked dances at monasteries such as Phodong and Rumtek, depicting stories of Guru Padmasambhava. On the day, an offering of chi-fut, a special drink, is made to the gods and an effigy of the demon king is burned. Then the social side begins: families visit each other, share feasts of meat, local greens and chhang, and there are archery contests in many villages.

For visitors, December gives cold, clear weather and quieter hotels than the October rush. Losoong is partly a home festival, so the public parts to look for are the monastery dances, community events in Gangtok and archery matches. Ask your hotel or driver which ones are open to visitors that year.
tips: Ask locally about archery contests, which are lively and usually happy to have quiet spectators.
Losoong is a public holiday in Sikkim, so expect some government offices and shops to close.
Pair Losoong with a Tsomgo Lake day trip for snow, but keep a buffer day in case the road shuts.

faqs.q: What is Losoong festival in Sikkim
faqs.a: Losoong, also called Sonam Losoong, is the harvest festival and new year of the Bhutia community of Sikkim, celebrated in December on the first day of the eleventh Tibetan month. The Lepchas celebrate it as Namsoong. It involves monastery dances beforehand, burning an effigy of evil, family feasts and traditional sports such as archery.

faqs.q: Is Losoong the same as Losar
faqs.a: No. Losar is the Tibetan new year in February or March. Losoong is the Sikkimese farmers' new year in December, after the harvest. The festival borrows some rituals from Losar, such as offerings and the burning of effigies, but it is a distinct Sikkimese celebration, especially among the Bhutia and Lepcha communities.

faqs.q: Where can tourists see Losoong celebrations
faqs.a: Look for masked dances at monasteries such as Phodong and Rumtek in the days before Losoong, and for the Kagyed dances at Tsuklakhang in Gangtok just before it. On and after the day, many villages hold archery contests and community events. Much of Losoong is celebrated at home, so ask your hotel or driver what is open to visitors.

faqs.q: Is December a good month for Gangtok
faqs.a: Yes, for clear views and value. December is dry and cold, about 5–15 °C in the day, with good Kangchenjunga views in the mornings. Hotels are quieter than in October and rates soften, except around Christmas and New Year. Snow can close the roads to Tsomgo and Nathu La for a few days, so check current status before you travel.
